text: Between 2001 and 2006, U.S. home prices rose by approximately 124 percent, fuelled by historically low interest rates set by the Federal Reserve following the dot-com crash and the 9/11 attacks. Lenders, eager to capitalise on the boom, issued mortgages to borrowers with poor credit histories — so-called subprime mortgages — often with adjustable rates that reset sharply upward after an introductory period. By 2005, roughly 20 percent of all new mortgages were subprime. Many borrowers were approved with little or no income verification under 'NINJA' (No Income, No Job, No Assets) loan standards.

The subprime mortgages were not held on bank balance sheets. Instead, banks bundled thousands of individual mortgages into mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and collateralised debt obligations (CDOs). These instruments were sold to investors worldwide, including pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and other banks. Rating agencies — Moody's, S&P, and Fitch — awarded AAA ratings to many of these products, incorrectly assuming that geographically diversified mortgage pools would not fail simultaneously. The fees generated by securitisation created a perverse incentive: originators profited from volume regardless of loan quality.

Starting in mid-2006, U.S. home prices began falling for the first time since the Great Depression. As prices dropped, homeowners with adjustable-rate mortgages found themselves owing more than their homes were worth — 'underwater' mortgages. Delinquency rates on subprime mortgages jumped from under 5 percent in 2005 to over 20 percent by early 2008. This triggered massive losses in the MBS and CDO markets, eroding the capital of every financial institution that held these securities.

Lehman Brothers, the fourth-largest U.S. investment bank, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on September 15, 2008 — the largest bankruptcy filing in U.S. history at the time, with $613 billion in debt. Lehman had accumulated roughly $85 billion in mortgage-related assets and had a leverage ratio of approximately 30:1 — meaning $30 borrowed for every $1 of equity. When the value of its mortgage portfolio fell, the firm could not meet its obligations. The U.S. Treasury and Federal Reserve declined to arrange a rescue, unlike the earlier bailout of Bear Stearns in March 2008.

Lehman's collapse triggered an immediate freeze in the interbank lending market. Banks became unwilling to lend to each other because no institution could reliably assess the counterparty risk of another bank's opaque mortgage holdings. The LIBOR-OIS spread — a key indicator of banking stress — spiked to 364 basis points in October 2008, compared with a pre-crisis level of around 10 basis points. Commercial paper markets also froze, cutting off short-term funding for thousands of corporations that relied on it for payroll and operations.

On October 3, 2008, President George W. Bush signed the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act, creating the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP) with $700 billion in authorised funding. TARP was initially intended to purchase toxic mortgage assets from banks, but Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson pivoted the strategy to direct capital injections into banks. By the end of 2008, $250 billion had been injected into financial institutions including Bank of America, Citigroup, JPMorgan Chase, and Goldman Sachs. The Federal Reserve also created unprecedented emergency lending facilities, including the Commercial Paper Funding Facility and the Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility.

The financial crisis transmitted to the real economy with devastating speed. U.S. GDP contracted 8.9 percent (annualised) in Q4 2008. The unemployment rate rose from 4.6 percent in 2007 to a peak of 10 percent in October 2009 — the highest level since 1983. Approximately 8.8 million jobs were lost between January 2008 and February 2010. The S&P 500 fell 57 percent from its October 2007 peak to its March 2009 trough. Global trade volumes fell by 12 percent in 2009, the steepest annual decline since World War II.

Post-crisis inquiries identified several systemic regulatory failures. The 1999 repeal of the Glass-Steagall Act (via the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act) allowed commercial banks to engage in investment banking activities, concentrating risk. The Securities and Exchange Commission's 2004 net capital rule exemption allowed the largest broker-dealers to increase leverage to as much as 40:1. The Office of Thrift Supervision failed to adequately supervise IndyMac and Washington Mutual, both of which failed in 2008. Credit rating agencies operated under a conflict of interest because issuers — not investors — paid for ratings.

In July 2010, President Obama signed the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, the most sweeping financial regulation since the 1930s. Key provisions included the Volcker Rule (restricting proprietary trading by banks), the creation of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), mandatory clearing of standardised derivatives through central counterparties, heightened capital and liquidity requirements for systemically important financial institutions (SIFIs), and the Orderly Liquidation Authority to wind down failing firms without taxpayer bailouts. Some economists argued the law did not go far enough; others said it over-regulated community banks.

The crisis spread rapidly beyond U.S. borders. European banks held significant quantities of U.S. mortgage-backed securities, and several — including UBS, Deutsche Bank, and BNP Paribas — reported large write-downs. Iceland's banking system, with assets worth ten times the country's GDP, collapsed entirely in October 2008, requiring an IMF bailout. Ireland, Greece, Portugal, and Spain subsequently faced sovereign debt crises linked to their domestic banking sectors, ultimately requiring Eurozone bailout programmes and severe austerity measures. The IMF estimated total global financial losses from the crisis at $4.1 trillion.
